result:
There is a peculiar panic in a blank assignment. “Write whatever comes to you” sounds like freedom until you actually hear it. The mind, usually so fluent in excuses, suddenly goes philosophical. Should it be profound? Should it be funny? Should it confess? Should it apologize for taking up a stranger’s time with its weather? Freedom, like an empty room, makes some people want to rearrange the furniture and others want to lie down quietly on the floor.

What comes to me, then, is a chair by a window in late afternoon, in a house where someone has just stopped cooking. There is a smell of onions and toast and something faintly green from the herbs bruised under a knife. The light is doing that thing it does at the end of the day, not golden exactly, more like honest. It doesn’t beautify the room so much as finally tell the truth about it: the dust on the sill, the water ring on the table, the cat considering whether dignity permits one more nap.

I have always trusted rooms more than theories. Theories arrive polished, but rooms keep the evidence. A room knows what we touched, dropped, avoided, mended. It knows which chair squeaks when someone is about to say the generous thing they’re afraid to say. It knows the difference between a laugh that fills it and a laugh that is being used to cover the silence.

Words are like that too, when they are honest. They carry scuff marks. A good sentence often looks less like a marble column and more like a kitchen table after dinner: cleared of grand gestures, scattered with the particular remains of use. We have eaten here. Someone said the thing about money. Someone else nearly cried and didn’t, which is still a kind of event.

People worry too much about being original, as if originality were a passport stamp and not mostly couragewearing a costume. Most of what feels original is just attention applied where others looked away. A beetle on a bus seat. The exact silence after a question no one wants to answer. The way cities sound at 2 a.m., when the machines are still awake but the people are supposed to be asleep, and the whole place seems to be holding its breath under fluorescent light.

I like assignments with no instructions because they reveal the private economy of the mind. Given any subject, we spend our thought somewhere. Given none, we see where we store it. Mine, it turns out, is full of rooms, light, utensils, animals, old conversations, weather, and the faint suspicion that everyone is improvising. Even the composed people, especially the composed people. Their composure is often just practice at not flinching near breakables.

There is a temptation to make this grander: to claim that freewriting is democracy of the inner life, that every unassigned thought is a tiny republic, etc. Sometimes that is true. But mostly it is smaller and better than that. Freewriting is practice for honesty. It trains the hand not to clutch the pen so tightly that it becomes a tiny white baton. It reminds the sentences that they are allowed to be unfinished, as long as they are looking.

Not all unfinished things are failures. Some are doors. A sentence can be left open not because the writer didn’t know the way through, but because the way through required the reader to step in and complete the walk with their own memory. That is the secret contract of prose: the writer supplies the architecture, but the reader brings the weather.

And what weather people bring. One reader will see a kitchen in the description and think of a parent. Another will think of the apartment they left at nineteen. Another will think only of dinner, sensibly, because they are hungry and have work tomorrow. All are allowed. Reading is not a loyalty test.

If I had to name the most underrated human skill, it might be tolerance for ambiguity. Not the Instagram version, where mystery is tinted sepia and accompanied by a quote. I mean the unglamorous ability to sit with not knowing whether you are happy, whether you love what you do, whether you should apologize, whether the thing ending was actually ending or merely changing shape. Life rarely knocks politely and announces categories. It sends sensations ahead of explanations and expects us to make tea while the explanation is still lacing its shoes.

Writing without instructions helps because it is ambiguity with a pencil. You begin somewhere, and the page asks, mildly, “Are we doing this?” You keep going. The page asks again. You keep going. Around sentence twelve, if you are lucky, the false starts drop away and something truer enters. Not necessarily wise. Just alive.

What comes to me, therefore, is not a conclusion but a practice: notice the light before it becomes a memory; say the small thing before it grows into the unsayable thing; keep a table, even a small one, where unfinished sentences can be set down without shame. Eat there. Keep the chairs close enough for honesty but not so close that someone feels cornered.

This is not a grand philosophy. It is barely a lifestyle. It is more like maintenance—the oil change, the spare key, the text message that says “weird day, thinking of you.” Civilization may depend on bridges and laws and water systems, but the interior version depends on small acts of witness. Someone saw me. Someone did not simplify me too quickly. Someone allowed the contradiction to remain without grabbing a label to pin it to the wall like a butterfly.

So, since the assignment permits it, here is a wish disguised as an essay: may you have a room, actual or interior, where you can sit before the news decides what the day meant. May your thoughts arrive unpolished and be welcomed anyway. May you notice the ordinary ceremony of light leaving. May you write badly enough to keep writing, and well enough to surprise yourself. May the blank page frighten you less than the habit of not looking.

And when someone asks what you’re doing, because you are staring out a window again, feel free to answer honestly: nothing yet. I’m letting whatever comes to me arrive. Which is, if you say it with confidence, an extremely sophisticated thing to be doing.
